group.passage:
Suppose a retired engineer spends an hour fixing a neighbor’s laptop. No money changes hands. Instead, she earns one time credit, which she spends a few weeks later when another member drives her to a hospital appointment and waits with her until she has seen the doctor. This simple exchange is the idea behind time banking.
The basic rule is that an hour of help earns one credit, whatever kind of help it is. An hour of legal advice is worth exactly the same as an hour of gardening or cooking. Similar ideas existed in the 1800s, but the term “time banking” was coined in 1980 by Edgar Cahn, an American law professor who hoped it would strengthen communities at a time when public services were being cut.
Time banks often grow when money is short. In Spain, where unemployment had reached nearly 25 percent, the number of time banks doubled in two years to almost 300, most with between 50 and 400 members. One mother in Madrid, whose teenage son uses a wheelchair, lost the daily help of a nurse when public spending was reduced. Now members of her time bank help lift her son, and she repays them by driving disabled neighbors in her specially fitted car.
In Canada, a time bank in the province of New Brunswick was started by a woman who had broken both of her wrists and needed help at home. Its members have traded rides to medical appointments, baking, snow clearing, and even skateboarding lessons. One board member likes to point out that asking for help is itself a way of helping, since it gives someone else a chance to earn hours.
That point matters more than it might seem. When researchers studied six time banks in England, they found that many members were glad to offer help but rarely asked for any, and as a result, activity slowed down. Most time banks do not last long, and those that survive usually have an organization behind them. In the end, a time bank depends as much on people willing to receive as on people willing to give.

translation_zh.text:
假設一位退休工程師花一個小時幫鄰居修筆電。過程中沒有任何金錢往來。她得到的是一點「時間點數」；幾週後，另一位成員開車載她去醫院看診，還陪她等到看完醫生，她就用掉這一點。這個簡單的交換，就是時間銀行背後的概念。
基本規則是：一小時的幫助換一點，不論是哪一種幫助。一小時的法律諮詢，和一小時的園藝或烹飪，價值完全相同。類似的構想在 1800 年代就已出現，但「時間銀行」這個名稱是美國法學教授艾德格‧卡恩在 1980 年創造的；當時公共服務正遭到刪減，他希望藉此強化社區。
時間銀行常在缺錢的時候成長。在西班牙，失業率一度將近 25%，時間銀行的數量在兩年內加倍，達到將近 300 家，大多數有 50 到 400 名成員。馬德里有一位母親，她十幾歲的兒子坐輪椅；公共支出縮減後，她失去了每天來幫忙的護理師。現在，時間銀行的成員幫忙抬她的兒子，她則開著特別改裝的車載送行動不便的鄰居作為回報。
在加拿大新布藍茲維省，有一家時間銀行是由一位女士創立的；她曾摔斷雙手手腕，需要有人到家裡幫忙。成員之間交換過載送看診、烘焙、鏟雪，甚至滑板課。一位董事常指出，開口求助本身就是一種幫忙，因為這讓別人有機會賺取時數。
這一點比看起來更重要。研究人員調查英格蘭的六家時間銀行時發現，許多成員樂於提供幫助，卻很少開口求助，結果交換活動因此變慢。大多數時間銀行都撐不久，能存活下來的通常有組織在背後支持。說到底，時間銀行既需要願意付出的人，也同樣需要願意接受的人。

open_tasks.prompt: Your neighborhood wants to start a time bank. Based on the passage, suggest one thing the organizers should do to keep it working, and explain why in 1–2 English sentences.
reference_answers: The organizers should remind members that asking for help is also a way of helping, because a time bank slows down when people only want to give.
They should find an organization such as a community center to support the time bank, since most time banks without one do not last long.
